SeriesLinearAlgAccessor::dot¶

Back to SeriesLinearAlgAccessor API Reference

Signatures¶

Series SeriesLinearAlgAccessor::dot(const Series& other) const
Series SeriesLinearAlgProxy::dot() const
Series Series::dot(const Series& other) const

What It Does¶

dot() computes the inner product of two one-dimensional Series.

For vectors x and y of length n:

dot(x, y) = x[0]y[0] + x[1]y[1] + ... + x[n-1]y[n-1]

The result is a rank-zero scalar because the vectors’ only dimension is fully reduced.

dot() does not conjugate complex values. If the left vector may be complex and the Hermitian inner product is intended, use vdot().

Pair, Multiply, Reduce¶

dot() measures alignment by pairing positions. Positive paired products add agreement, negative paired products subtract it, and orthogonal vectors cancel to zero. It is not elementwise multiplication because no vector dimension survives: every paired product is reduced into one scalar.

The operation is bilinear. Scaling either input scales the result by the same factor, and scaling the scalar result scales both reverse sensitivities.

Parameter¶

other (const Series&) The right vector. Both operands must be one-dimensional and have the same length. Their elementwise multiplication must also have a valid common dtype and platform.

Returns¶

Series A rank-zero scalar Series containing the sum of paired products.

Gradient¶

For real vectors and scalar objective L = dot(x, y):

dL/dx = y
dL/dy = x

If dot() is part of a larger expression with incoming scalar sensitivity g, both results are scaled by g.

dL/dx = g y
dL/dy = g x

Examples¶

Example 1. Pair corresponding vector positions, then sum.

auto left = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0});
auto right = pluss::make_series({10.0, 20.0, 30.0, 40.0});

std::cout << left.linearalg.dot(right) << "\n";

The scalar is

1*10 + 2*20 + 3*30 + 4*40 = 300

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=300

Example 2. Both input vectors receive the other vector as sensitivity.

auto x = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0});
auto y = pluss::make_series({4.0, 5.0, 6.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);
y.tracks_slope_(true);

x.linearalg.dot(y).reverse();

std::cout << "dL_dx=" << x.sensitivity() << "\n";
std::cout << "dL_dy=" << y.sensitivity() << "\n";

Output¶

dL_dx=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[4, 5, 6]
dL_dy=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 2, 3]

Example 3. An upstream scalar multiplier becomes the incoming sensitivity for the dot product.

auto x = pluss::make_series({1.0, -2.0, 3.0});
auto y = pluss::make_series({4.0, 5.0, -1.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);
y.tracks_slope_(true);

x.linearalg.dot(y).mul(2.5).reverse();

std::cout << "value=" << x.linearalg.dot(y) << "\n";
std::cout << "dL_dx=" << x.sensitivity() << "\n";
std::cout << "dL_dy=" << y.sensitivity() << "\n";

The unscaled dot product is 4 - 10 - 3 = -9. The objective is 2.5 * dot(x, y), so the sensitivities are 2.5*y and 2.5*x.

Output¶

value=pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=-9
dL_dx=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[10, 12.5, -2.5]
dL_dy=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[2.5, -5, 7.5]

Example 4. Orthogonal vectors produce zero through cancellation, not because either vector is zero.

std::cout << pluss::make_series({2.0, 1.0}).linearalg.dot(
    pluss::make_series({-1.0, 2.0})) << "\n";

Here 2*(-1) + 1*2 = 0.

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=0

Example 5. Matrices are rejected even when they contain the same number of elements.

try {
  std::cout << pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0}}).linearalg.dot(
      pluss::make_series({{3.0, 4.0}})) << "\n";
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::cout << e.what() << "\n";
}

Output¶

dot: expected two 1D Series

Example 6. Vector lengths must match.

try {
  std::cout << pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0}).linearalg.dot(
      pluss::make_series({3.0, 4.0, 5.0})) << "\n";
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::cout << e.what() << "\n";
}

Output¶

dot: inputs must have the same length

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • Both operands must be one-dimensional. Reshape explicitly before calling if transforming a matrix into a vector is genuinely part of the algorithm.

  • Equal element count is not a substitute for the one-dimensional contract.

  • Vector lengths must match; there is no broadcasting.

  • Complex dot() does not conjugate either input.

Summary¶

dot() is a strict vector inner product: pair positions, multiply, sum, and return a scalar. Use vdot() when conjugating the left complex vector is required.
